text:
**For most full-size fridges, get a station with at least 1,200–1,500 W of surge and about 1,000 Wh of capacity for most of a day, or 1,500–2,000 Wh for a full 24 hours.**

## Check 1: Can it start and run the fridge?
- **Surge (peak) watts.** The compressor pulls a short spike when it starts, usually around 1,000–1,800 W for a standard fridge and up to about 2,400 W for large French-door or older models ([BlackBoxSupplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). HomeGridHQ recommends clearing 1,200 W ([source](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)), and powerstations.reviews uses 1,300 W ([source](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). If the surge rating is too low, the station shuts off the moment the fridge starts, no matter how big its battery is.
- **Continuous watts.** A fridge draws about 100–250 W while running, which almost any 1,000 W-class station can handle.
- **Pure sine wave output.** Compressors can run badly on "modified sine" inverters. All major brands use pure sine wave.

## Check 2: How long will it last?
The compressor only runs about 30–40% of the time, so the average draw is much lower than the label wattage. A typical full-size fridge averages about 40–70 W.

**To calculate your own fridge's needs**, use the kWh/year figure on its yellow EnergyGuide label:
1. Divide kWh/year by 8,760, then multiply by 1,000. That gives average watts.
2. Multiply by 24 hours and by the number of days.
3. Divide by 0.85 for inverter losses, then multiply by 1.2 for headroom.

**Example:** A 362 kWh/yr fridge averages 41 W. It needs about **1,400 Wh for one day** and **2,800 Wh for two days** ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

**Rough runtimes** for a typical fridge ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)):

| Station size | Approx. fridge runtime |
|---|---|
| ~1,000 Wh | ~16–17 hours |
| ~1,500 Wh | ~24 hours |
| ~2,000 Wh | ~33 hours |
| ~3,000 Wh | ~2 days |

Large side-by-side fridges with ice makers can use about twice as much energy. Keeping the door shut stretches runtime a lot.

## Options that pass both checks
- **About 1 kWh, for short outages:** The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, about $499) and the Bluetti AC180 (1,152 Wh, 2,700 W peak) both appear in [BlackBoxSupplies' picks](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). My search results didn't include a direct store link for either.
- **About 2 kWh, for a full day or more:**
  - **Anker SOLIX S2000:** 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W continuous, 3,000 W peak, $699.99 after coupon. [Buy at Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator)
  - **BLUETTI AC200L:** 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W continuous, expandable to about 8 kWh, $899. A listing reports code AFF5OFF takes 5% off, bringing it to about $854. [Buy via Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac200l). This is an affiliate link and the code isn't guaranteed.

**Tip:** Test your fridge on the station before an outage to confirm it starts reliably.
